content.text:
Now I can give you a real answer.

**Your framing is right — "a skill is a Behavior the agent invokes rather than a trigger."** Both are prompt + metadata; the only difference is who decides when it runs. And `triggers` is already optional, so a trigger-less Behavior is legal today.

**But the piece that would make it work doesn't exist.** There's no `run_behavior` tool — no way for an agent to invoke a Behavior mid-conversation. Behaviors are fired by events and schedules only. So a trigger-less Behavior today isn't a skill; it's a Behavior that never runs.

That gap is the whole idea, and it's small:

- Add an agent-facing tool to invoke a Behavior by slug
- Read `SKILL.md` files into Behaviors at `lobu apply` (you already parse frontmatter for `skillFromFile`)
- Delete `skills_config`, the `.skills/` materialization, `SkillsInstructionProvider`, and the 17-file UI

You'd keep the industry-standard `SKILL.md` on disk — so portability and vocabulary survive — while collapsing two concepts into one internally. Behaviors already have UI, `apply` support, versioning, and entity promotion; skills have a bespoke tab and a jsonb blob.

The honest catch: progressive disclosure. Skills currently inject one summary line and let the agent read the body on demand. A Behavior's `prompt` is the whole thing. To match, invocation would need to load the body at call time rather than inline it — which the tool would do naturally, but it's the detail that decides whether this saves tokens or costs them.

So: **genuinely promising, and the right shape** — one concept, two invocation modes, standard file format preserved. Not something to start now, though. It's a design change with an unbuilt tool at its centre, and #2290 is sitting green waiting to merge.

content.text:
This is a useful data point, and it lands on your side of the argument.

**Flue keeps skills as a distinct primitive** — separate from tools, separate from agents. Declared as `SKILL.md` files, imported explicitly:

```js
import triage from '../skills/triage/SKILL.md' with { type: 'skill' }
```

Then composed into an agent's context alongside models and tools. And they're distributable as npm packages.

Three things that bear on your decisions:

**Skills aren't folded into a job primitive.** Flue treats them as their own layer — reusable expertise, not triggered work. That's evidence against both "delete skills" and "rename Behaviors to skills." Your instinct that these are different things matches how the category is settling.

**The file format is converging.** `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` is exactly your layout. Anthropic's Agent Skills use it too. That's now a de-facto standard, and you already conform — which is real portability, not just vocabulary.

**Explicit composition, not implicit attachment.** Flue *imports* a skill into an agent's context rather than attaching it via config. That's closer to your `@`-mention idea than to `agents.skills_config` — the reference sits where the guidance is used.

What I couldn't determine: whether Flue does progressive disclosure. Your implementation injects a summary line and loads `SKILL.md` on demand, which may be more sophisticated than theirs — I'd want to verify before assuming either way.

So on your original question — is it best to keep skills? The industry answer is yes, and keeping them as-is conforms. The idea genuinely worth revisiting later is the `@`-mention/import model, since two independent frameworks landed on explicit composition rather than config attachment.

content.text:
Flue splits triggering into three layers, and the comparison to yours is instructive:

**Channels** handle incoming events — they verify authenticity (webhook signatures and such) before dispatching to an agent. That's your connector layer's job.

**Triggers** are file-based routing with webhook and schedule metadata, consumed by an external scheduler. So Flue *declares* the schedule but delegates running it.

**Durable Streams** are the interesting part: every event, prompt, tool response, and model choice goes into an append-only log. If a process dies, another picks up the log and resumes at the exact step.

Two things worth noting against your architecture:

Your **Behaviors merge Flue's channels and triggers into one primitive** — a Behavior declares both what it subscribes to and what it does. Flue separates the transport (channel) from the subscription (trigger). Yours is fewer concepts; theirs is more composable.

And you already have the durable-log idea — that's your `events` append-only table, with the same never-DELETE invariant. Flue applies it at the agent-step level for crash resumption; you apply it at the domain-event level for entity promotion. Same primitive, different altitude.

So the honest read: **Flue validates your Behavior model rather than challenging it.** Both have skills as passive reference material and a separate triggered-execution path. Nobody in the category is folding the two together, which is more evidence for the conclusion we already reached — leave skills alone.

Sources: [Better Stack: Flue framework guide](https://betterstack.com/community/guides/ai/flue-framework/), [Cloudflare Blog: Flue SDK](https://blog.cloudflare.com/agents-platform-flue-sdk/), [GitHub - withastro/flue](https://github.com/withastro/flue), [Flue — The Open Agent Framework](https://flueframework.com/)

Some of your complexity is warranted by problems they haven't hit; some is genuinely accidental. Only reading both tells you which is which.

input.prompt: Describe Flue's architecture concretely: What are its core primitives (agents, skills, tools, channels, triggers)? How is an agent defined and executed? What is the execution/runtime model — is there a durable event log, how does it resume after crash? How does sandboxing work? Is it single-tenant or multi-tenant? What is the repo structure and package layout? Include any code examples showing agent/skill definition.

content.content:
# Flue Architecture Overview

## Core Primitives

Flue's architecture centers on these key components:

**Agents**: Autonomous entities that maintain context across conversations. As described, "The agent IS the function" — agents are TypeScript functions decorated with `'use agent'` that compose their complete execution harness.

**Skills**: Reusable expertise packages (markdown-based) that agents load for specialized guidance. The framework enables agents to "load whenever a task needs specialized guidance."

**Tools**: Typed actions for controlled interactions with external systems. Tools grant "agents the context and autonomy to solve complex tasks."

**Channels**: Event sources from platforms like Slack, Teams, Discord, GitHub. These "receive verified events" to trigger agent work.

**Sandboxes**: Secure execution environments where agents "can use tools, modify files, and autonomously complete real work" — supporting local, virtual, or remote containers.

## Agent Definition & Execution

Agents are defined as TypeScript functions using composition hooks:

```typescript
export function Triage() {
  useModel('anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6');
  useSandbox(local());
  useSkill(triage);
  useSkill(verify);
  useTool(openIssue);
  useTool(searchCode);
  return `Task instructions...`;
```

# Flue Architecture Overview

## Core Primitives

Flue's architecture centers on these key components:

**Agents**: Autonomous entities that maintain context across conversations. As described, "The agent IS the function" — agents are TypeScript functions decorated with `'use agent'` that compose their complete execution harness.

**Skills**: Reusable expertise packages (markdown-based) that agents load for specialized guidance. The framework enables agents to "load whenever a task needs specialized guidance."

**Tools**: Typed actions for controlled interactions with external systems. Tools grant "agents the context and autonomy to solve complex tasks."

**Channels**: Event sources from platforms like Slack, Teams, Discord, GitHub. These "receive verified events" to trigger agent work.

**Sandboxes**: Secure execution environments where agents "can use tools, modify files, and autonomously complete real work" — supporting local, virtual, or remote containers.

## Agent Definition & Execution

Agents are defined as TypeScript functions using composition hooks:

```typescript
export function Triage() {
  useModel('anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6');
  useSandbox(local());
  useSkill(triage);
  useSkill(verify);
  useTool(openIssue);
  useTool(searchCode);
  return `Task instructions...`;
}
```

This pattern treats "the agent as the function" — the harness is declaratively composed within it.

The documentation mentions durability features where agents "preserve progress through failures and restarts with durable recovery for accepted work," though specifics on event logging aren't detailed in the provided content.

My honest recommendation: **merge #2290, then stop.** This session has been heavily skills-focused for a feature with two internal users. The knob-simplification instinct would pay off more on a surface people actually use.

content.text:
Here's the honest comparison for autonomy.

**They're solving different halves, and you have the harder one.**

Flue's autonomy story is *composition*: `useSandbox(local())`, `useSkill(triage)`, `useTool(openIssue)` — declare the agent's capabilities as code, hand it a goal, let it run. Elegant, and the whole thing lives in one function.

But scan what you have that their docs never mention: **82 files touching approvals, 92 touching schedules, 59 touching job queues, 40 touching resume/checkpoint.** Plus `manage_operations` and `entity-field-approval` — a human-in-the-loop gate where an agent proposes a write and a person confirms.

That's not incidental complexity. **Fully autonomous agents fail on the operational half, not the composition half.** An agent that runs once in your repo needs `useTool`. An agent running unattended on a schedule for 66 orgs needs: what happens when it dies mid-run, what it's allowed to do without asking, what happens when it proposes something wrong, and how you audit it after.

You've built all four. Flue's docs describe "durable recovery for accepted work" without saying how.

**What's genuinely worth stealing — one thing:**

Composition-as-code. `useSkill(triage)` colocates the capability with the agent that uses it; your `skills_config` jsonb separates them, which is exactly the awkwardness driving this whole session. The `@`-mention idea you raised was reaching for the same property.

**What I'd caution against:**

Their model assumes single-tenant and local imports. `useSkill(triage)` resolves at build time in your repo. Yours resolves at runtime, for an org, on a shared worker. You can't copy the ergonomics without giving that up.

**The uncomfortable observation:** the biggest gap to fully autonomous isn't architecture — it's that your approval gate is currently the *only* thing between an agent and a bad write. The `jobType:exec` note in your memory says `handleExecJob` spawns `sh -c` on the host, bypassing D1 guards. That's a concrete autonomy blocker sitting in your own notes, and it's more consequential than anything Flue does differently.

I'd rather dig into that than keep comparing frameworks — but #2290 first; `pi-review` is still resolving.

**FINAL 2026-07-29 — read this, the rest is archaeology.** Skill-declared guardrails are GONE (#2290 → `1f0cb2d9`, −763/+70, verified live in main's source). A guardrail is OPERATOR intent; a skill is CAPABILITY content. Merging them let a content author write security policy for every agent enabling their skill — which is why the precedence rule, the hashed inline name, and #2285's validation all existed. Zero prod skills used it and no UI ever exposed it. Also removed: `contentFetchedAt` + `providers` (dead), and the aggregator's `names` return field (zero prod readers, allocated per call on the tools/call path). KEPT `modelPreference`/`thinkingLevel` — the line is **advisory vs enforcing**, not config vs content: those render into prompt text the model may ignore; guardrails could BLOCK a tool call. **TRAP that cost a review round: deleting `validateSkillsConfigGuardrails` also deleted the STRUCTURAL checks, leaving `skillsConfig` with no write validation — `enabled:"yes"` persisted where it used to 400, and the runtime gates on truthiness (`s.enabled &&`). Restored as a shallow `validateSkillsConfig`. When deleting a validator, check what non-target checks live inside it.** **SKILLS THEMSELVES STAY.** Track 3 ($skill entity) is SHELVED, not pending: prod has 2 skill rows, duplication factor 1.00, zero divergence — the premise was false. Also the `$` prefix would hide the type from the entity rail (`isSystemEntityType`), and the generic board CANNOT author markdown (`DynamicSchemaForm` renders every string as a single-line Input; `entities.content` isn't even readable in the web API), so "delete the bespoke UI" is a downgrade. The skills tab (17 files, 4 routes) is untouched and must stay until something else can author a SKILL.md. Industry check: Flue (Astro team) and Anthropic both use `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` as passive reference material with a separate triggered-execution path — nobody folds skills into a job primitive, so DON'T rename Behaviors to skills and DON'T fold them together. Notably Flue builds on the SAME Pi harness we do, so it's not core-vs-core: they have nicer composition ergonomics (`useSkill(triage)` colocates capability with agent) over a single-tenant problem; we have the operational half they don't document (82 files touching approvals, 92 schedules, 40 resume/checkpoint). The one idea worth stealing is composition-as-code. Related: [[feedback_text_matcher_is_never_the_boundary]].
